lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: understand how vaccination results in the manufacture of memory cells, which enable future antibody production to the pathogen to occur sooner, faster and in greater quantity

primer.text: A vaccine teaches your immune system a threat it has never met. Harmless pathogen fragments parade past your lymphocytes, memory cells form, and the real pathogen — arriving years later — meets an army already mobilised. This note explains the preparation and the graph it produces.

modules.title: What Goes Into a Vaccine
modules.opening: Vaccines contain harmless versions of a pathogen — killed, weakened, or mere fragments — delivered by injection, orally or nasally, so the body can build immunity without ever suffering the disease.
keyPoints: Vaccines hold harmless versions of the pathogen.
The pathogen may be killed, attenuated, or present only as fragments.
Delivery routes include oral, nasal and injection.
Widespread vaccination has reduced or eradicated diseases.
The harmless form still carries the antigens that trigger immunity.

low.restatement: A vaccine shows the immune system a disarmed copy of the enemy and lets it train.
low.analogy: A fire drill with a staged, controlled flame — no building burns, everyone learns the exits.
low.examPointer: List all three harmlessness strategies; naming one only is a common slip.

medium.restatement: Because the antigen markers survive on the harmless form, lymphocytes respond exactly as they would to the real pathogen, minus the disease.
medium.analogy: Practising against a shadow boxer: the moves are real, the punches are not.
medium.examPointer: Use the word antigens when explaining why a killed pathogen still works.

modules.title: Memory Cells and the Faster Response
modules.opening: Once the vaccine's antigens reach the bloodstream, lymphocytes respond with specific antibodies and produce memory cells that persist for years, so any future infection meets a response that arrives sooner, runs faster and in greater quantity.
keyPoints: Antibodies specific to those antigens are produced.
Memory cells form from the activated lymphocytes.
Memory cells and antibodies circulate long afterwards.
A later infection triggers a faster, larger response.

low.restatement: Train once with the harmless form; the memory cells remember and answer instantly next time.
low.analogy: A spelling bee: having drilled the word, you spell it at speed when the judge calls it.
low.examPointer: Quote the triple: sooner, faster and in greater quantity.

medium.restatement: Because memory cells persist, the secondary response outpaces the pathogen's reproduction, so disease never establishes and the person is immune.
medium.analogy: A town that drilled its fire brigade once puts out the second fire before it spreads.
medium.examPointer: Tie 'immune' to the pathogen failing to cause disease despite entry.

glossary.definition: A harmless pathogen preparation that builds immunity without disease.
The surface marker that the immune system recognises as foreign.
Long-lasting lymphocytes that enable a faster future response.
Protected so that a pathogen cannot cause disease.
